exam: What demographic indicator would you examine first to decide if a district needs more antenatal clinics? — Look at the crude birth rate and proportion of women aged 15‑49; a high rate signals need for expanded services.

A rural hospital reports a sudden increase in under‑5 deaths. Which demographic factor should you investigate and why? — Examine recent changes in birth rate and migration; a surge may reflect overcrowding or loss of preventive programs.

How does rapid urban migration affect the burden of non‑communicable disease in a low‑resource setting? — Urban migrants often adopt sedentary lifestyles and processed diets, raising hypertension and diabetes prevalence, while health services may remain geared to infectious disease.

Explain why a high proportion of elderly patients can strain a district hospital’s resources even if overall population size is stable. — Elderly patients need chronic‑disease management, polypharmacy monitoring, and rehabilitation, which require staff time and medicines not accounted for in a young‑population model.

When a verbal autopsy suggests malaria as a leading cause of death, what immediate public‑health action is justified? — Scale up rapid diagnostic testing and distribution of insecticide‑treated nets; prioritize antimalarial drug stocks.

Distinguish between ‘crude death rate’ and ‘age‑specific death rate’ and state which is more useful for evaluating child health programs. — Crude death rate counts all deaths per 1,000 population; age‑specific death rate focuses on a defined age group (e.g., under‑5). The latter directly reflects child health interventions.

A health‑facility register shows a decline in reported births but community surveys show stable fertility. What could explain this discrepancy? — Possible under‑reporting due to home deliveries, loss of records, or migration of pregnant women to other facilities.

Why might a high population growth rate mask a falling infant mortality rate in a district’s health report? — Absolute numbers of infant deaths may stay high despite a lower proportion, giving a false impression of unchanged mortality.
ai.title: Demography and Population Health
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Demography studies population size, structure, and change, informing disease burden and health service planning. Clinicians use demographic data to anticipate common conditions and allocate limited resources in low‑resource settings.

b: Birth rate = live births per 1,000 population per year
Death rate = deaths per 1,000 population per year
Crude migration rate = net migrants per 1,000 population per year
sections.p: Demography quantifies births, deaths, migration, and age‑sex composition of a defined population. In clinical practice it is derived from census data, health‑facility registers, and community surveys.

b: Stage I: high birth & death rates, low life expectancy
Stage II: falling death rates, rising life expectancy
Stage III: declining birth rates, ageing population
sections.p: Population health impact is staged by demographic transition: pre‑transition (high fertility, high mortality), transition (falling mortality), and post‑transition (low fertility, ageing).

b: HIV/AIDS reducing adult survival
Malaria and TB affecting child mortality
Improved vaccination lowering infant deaths
Rural‑to‑urban migration altering age structure

Older population → hypertension, diabetes, stroke
sections.p: Clinicians encounter demographic patterns as clusters of disease: high childhood diarrhoea in rapidly growing populations, or rising non‑communicable disease in ageing urban cohorts.

sections.p: Demography is sometimes mixed up with epidemiology, but epidemiology studies disease patterns, whereas demography describes the underlying population structure.
